scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: Government should actively shape the economy to serve the community, not just referee a free market.
A strong social safety net is compatible with, and even expresses, conservative values of care for one's own.
Protecting domestic industry and workers can justify departing from free-market orthodoxy.
The state has a legitimate role in supporting families and communities against pure market pressures.
Economic policy should serve social stability, even where that means limiting market forces.
A conservative government should be willing to intervene economically to protect its own people and institutions.
Free markets, left largely alone, are the best mechanism for producing widely shared prosperity.
Government intervention in the economy usually does more harm than the problems it's meant to fix.
Lower taxes and less regulation are generally the right conservative default.
A dynamic, competitive market economy is itself a conservative value worth protecting from state overreach.
Economic freedom and limited government go together as core conservative commitments.
The state should mainly get out of the way and let markets and individual enterprise do the work.
A country should actively use its power abroad to defend its interests and allies, even through military means.
Standing by while threats to the international order grow unchecked is itself a dangerous policy.
Strength and willingness to act abroad deters aggression better than restraint does.
A great power has responsibilities beyond its own borders that sometimes require intervention.
Isolationism leaves a vacuum that hostile powers are happy to fill.
Credible military commitments abroad are a core part of national strength.
Foreign wars and entanglements rarely serve the actual national interest and should be avoided.
A country's first duty is to its own people, not to policing the rest of the world.
Restraint abroad conserves the resources and cohesion a nation needs at home.
Nation-building efforts overseas have mostly failed and shouldn't be repeated.
A modest, defensive foreign policy serves the nation better than an interventionist one.
Foreign entanglements distract from and drain resources away from problems at home.
Public life can be conducted on shared civic and moral terms without appeal to any particular religious tradition.
A pluralist society is better served by secular civic institutions than by religiously grounded ones.
Conservatism does not require religious belief; a secular tradition of prudence and order is enough.
Public policy should be justified in terms accessible to believers and non-believers alike.
Religious institutions should stay out of formal political power, whatever moral influence they retain informally.
A conservative order can rest on custom and civic virtue without needing a religious foundation.
A society's moral order should be explicitly grounded in religious faith and tradition.
Religious institutions and teaching deserve a formal, protected place in public life.
A nation's laws and public morality lose their foundation once they're cut off from religious grounding.
Faith communities should have real influence over policies touching family, life, and public morality.
A confessional foundation gives a society's moral order a stability that secular reasoning alone cannot.
Public education and law should reflect the religious tradition of the community, not stand apart from it.
National identity should be open to anyone who embraces the country's civic institutions and values, regardless of ancestry.
Shared commitment to a country's constitution and civic culture, not shared ancestry, is what makes someone a member of the nation.
Immigrants who adopt the nation's institutions and civic values are as fully members of it as anyone born there.
A nation is best understood as a community of citizens united by law and creed.
What binds a nation together is allegiance to its principles, not descent from a common stock.
Citizenship, properly earned, confers full national belonging regardless of ethnic background.
A nation is fundamentally a people with a shared ancestry, culture, and history, not just a set of institutions.
Large-scale demographic change poses a real threat to a nation's cultural continuity.
A country's historic ethnic and cultural core deserves special protection and priority.
National identity is inherited, not simply chosen by anyone who adopts the country's institutions.
Preserving a nation's traditional cultural character is a legitimate goal of immigration policy.
A common ancestry and cultural inheritance are what make a people a nation, more than any legal document.
Institutions should be reformed gradually and cautiously, correcting flaws without discarding what works.
Prudent, incremental adjustment is the responsible conservative approach to a changing world.
Change should be tested and reversible, not sweeping and irreversible.
A conservative should be willing to reform institutions that have genuinely stopped serving their purpose.
Careful, piecemeal improvement respects both the wisdom of the past and the needs of the present.
Conservatism at its best manages change rather than simply resisting it.
Society has drifted so far from its proper order that a real restoration, not just gradual correction, is needed.
Many of the last century's changes were net losses that deserve to be reversed, not merely managed.
Cautious reform is inadequate when the institutions themselves have been captured by the wrong values.
A return to an earlier, sounder order is a legitimate political goal, not mere nostalgia.
What's needed now is restoration, not incremental adjustment within a fundamentally compromised system.
Gradualism is too slow a response to how far things have already gone wrong.
Government should be kept small, with most decisions left to individuals, families, and local communities.
Centralised state power, even used for conservative ends, tends to outgrow its original purpose.
A conservative should be as wary of an activist state as of a radical one.
Power should be devolved downward whenever possible, away from central government.
Local and voluntary institutions handle most social problems better than a central bureaucracy does.
The instinct to expand state authority, whatever the intent behind it, deserves conservative suspicion.
A strong, capable central state is necessary to defend the national order and enforce its values.
Conservatives should be willing to use state power decisively, not just resist its growth.
Effective governance sometimes requires a strong executive able to act without being bogged down by every institutional check.
A weak state cannot actually protect the traditions and order conservatives care about.
Directing state power toward explicitly conservative ends is a legitimate and necessary strategy.
Institutional gridlock is as much an enemy of good order as an overreaching state.
Moral order in society is best sustained through persuasion, example, and civil institutions, not legal compulsion.
The law should stay fairly neutral on questions of personal and family morality.
Cultural and moral renewal has to come from within communities and institutions, not from legislation.
Using the law to enforce a particular moral vision usually backfires and breeds resentment.
Civil society — family, church, community — should carry the weight of moral formation, not the state.
Persuasion within a free society is a more legitimate route to moral order than legal coercion.
The law should actively uphold and enforce the community's moral and social order, not remain neutral on it.
Legal enforcement of core moral norms — around family, life, and public decency — is a proper role of government.
A society that refuses to legislate morality has already lost the fight over what its public order should be.
Some questions of right and wrong are too important to leave to persuasion alone; the law has to take a side.
Protecting the moral fabric of society sometimes requires using the law, not just cultural argument.
A conservative government should be willing to legislate its moral convictions, not just hold them privately.
Experienced, established leaders and institutions should generally be trusted over popular anger at them.
Political stability depends on deference to competent, tested institutions rather than constant upheaval.
Conservatism is fundamentally about preserving established authority, not overturning it in the name of the people.
Elite expertise, however imperfect, usually outperforms populist mobilisation at actual governing.
A conservative should be suspicious of movements that promise to sweep away the existing establishment entirely.
Respect for established institutions and their leadership is itself a conservative virtue.
The existing political and cultural establishment has betrayed ordinary people and deserves to be swept aside.
Popular anger at entrenched elites is a legitimate and healthy political force, not something to be managed away.
Mobilising ordinary people against an unresponsive establishment is a legitimate conservative strategy.
Elites who no longer represent the nation's real interests and values have forfeited their claim to deference.
A movement that channels popular grievance against the establishment can be a genuinely conservative one.
Established institutions have drifted so far from the public they serve that they no longer deserve automatic trust.
